questions.question: A single server has service times $S_k$; let $U_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_k$, $U(t)=\max\{k\colon U_k\leq t\}$, let $D(t)$ count the jobs that actually leave in $[0,t]$ and $A(t)$ the arrivals in $[0,t]$. Which limit defines the service rate $\mu$?
options: $\mu=\lim_{t\to\infty}D(t)/t$, the long-run number of actual departures per unit time
$\mu=\lim_{n\to\infty}U_n/n$, the long-run total service time per job served
$\mu=\lim_{t\to\infty}U(t)/t$, completions per unit time if the server never stood idle
$\mu=\lim_{t\to\infty}A(t)/t$, the long-run number of jobs offered per unit time

questions.question: At a single server, every type of job is replaced by a job that needs on average twice as much service time, so the mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ doubles while the arrival stream stays the same. What happens to the service rate $\mu$?
options: $\mu$ halves, since $\mu=1/\mathbb{E}[S]$ is a number of jobs per unit time
$\mu$ doubles, since the server now spends twice as long per job
$\mu$ stays the same, since it is a property of the server alone
$\mu$ halves only if the server is always busy; otherwise it is unchanged

questions.question: For a single-server queue with arrival rate $\lambda$ and service times $S_k$, what determines the service rate $\mu$ of the server?
options: The load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, the work brought to the server per unit time
The long-run fraction of time during which the server is busy
The maximum number of jobs allowed in the system at the same time
The service times alone, through the mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$ of a single service

questions.question: A single server without blocking has service rate $\mu$ and departure rate $\delta$. In the long run it is idle a quarter of the time because no jobs are present then. How do $\delta$ and $\mu$ compare?
options: $\delta=\mu$, because the service rate is the observed output rate
$\delta<\mu$, because no jobs are completed during the idle time
$\mu<\delta$, because $\mu$ also averages over the idle time
$\delta=\lambda=\mu$, because every job eventually leaves the system

questions.question: For a single server with service times $S_k$, let $U(t)=\max\{k\colon U_k\leq t\}$ with $U_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_k$, and suppose $U(t)/t\to\mu\in(0,\infty)$. What does $t/U(t)$ approach as $t\to\infty$?
options: The mean time between actual departures, $1/\delta$
The mean length of a busy period of the server

questions.question: A ticket machine serves one customer at a time, with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=45$ seconds. What is its service rate $\mu$ in customers per hour?

Jobs arrive as a Poisson process at a single server, and the service times are $S\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ with service rate $\mu=3$ jobs per hour. What is the probability $\mathbb{P}(S>20\text{ min})$ that a service lasts longer than $20$ minutes?
A job requires work $s_k=6$ units. It is processed by server $i$, which works at rate $\mu(i)=1.5$ units of work per time unit. How long does the job take at this server?
A pharmacy counter has $c=3$ identical pharmacists working in parallel, each with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=12$ minutes. What is the capacity of the counter, in customers per hour?

A ferry carries on average $\mathbb{E}[C]=25$ cars per crossing, and a full round trip takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=40$ minutes, after which it loads again. Treating the ferry as one batch server, what is its service rate in cars per hour?

A single server, empty at time $0$, serves jobs one at a time; $S_k$ is the service time of the $k$th job it serves, $\mu=\lim U(t)/t$ with $U(t)=\max\{k\colon S_1+\dots+S_k\leq t\}$, and $\delta$ is its departure rate. Why does $\delta\leq\mu$ hold for every arrival pattern?
options: Because the bound assumes $\lambda<\mu$, and the departure rate never exceeds $\lambda$
Because the server is work-conserving, so it is never idle while jobs wait
Because service times are exponential, so completions form a Poisson stream
Because $n$ departures need total service $S_1+\dots+S_n\leq t$, so $D(t)\leq U(t)$

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single first-come-first-served server with arrival rate $\lambda$ smaller than its service rate $\mu$, and no job is blocked. Let $U(t)$ be the number of jobs the server would complete in $[0,t]$ without interruption and $D(t)$ the number that actually leave. With departure rate $\delta<\mu$, the difference $U(t)-D(t)$ grows roughly like $(\mu-\delta)t$. What does it measure?
options: Jobs the server could have completed during its idle time if work had been there
Jobs that are waiting in the queue at time $t$, which pile up over time
Jobs that were turned away because the server was busy when they arrived
A backlog showing the queue is unstable, since the difference is unbounded

questions.question: The service times $S_k$ of a single server are iid with $0<\mathbb{E}[S]<\infty$; let $U_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_k$ and $U(t)=\max\{k\colon U_k\leq t\}$. Which argument shows that the service rate $\mu=\lim_{t\to\infty}U(t)/t$ exists and equals $1/\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: The queue must be stable, $\lambda<1/\mathbb{E}[S]$; otherwise $U(t)/t$ grows without bound and the limit does not exist
The $S_k$ must be exponential, so that the completions of a non-stop server form a Poisson process with rate $1/\mathbb{E}[S]$
By the strong law of large numbers $U_n/n\to\mathbb{E}[S]$, and the counting argument of Theorem 4.1.1 gives $U(t)/t\to1/\mathbb{E}[S]$
The server must be work-conserving; otherwise its idle time enters $U(t)$ and the limit falls below $1/\mathbb{E}[S]$

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a first-come-first-served single server, empty at time $0$, at times $2,4,10,12,18,20,\dots$, and each needs exactly $3$ time units of service. With $U(t)=\max\{k\colon 3k\leq t\}$ the uninterrupted completion count and $D(t)$ the number of actual departures in $[0,t]$, what are $U(15)$ and $D(15)$?

During an $8$-hour shift a single server, empty at the start and at the end of the shift, completes $30$ jobs. It is idle $25\%$ of the shift and otherwise serves exactly these $30$ jobs. What is the estimated service rate $\mu$?

In a discrete-time queue the capacity per day $c_k$ is $8$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, $12$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ and $0$ (machine down) with probability $\frac{1}{4}$; the mean number of arrivals per day is $\lambda=7.5$. What are $\mu=\mathbb{E}[c_k]$ and the sign of the drift $\lambda-\mu$?

A single server without blocking has arrival rate $\lambda$ larger than its service rate $\mu$. It pauses for $10$ minutes every hour, even when jobs are waiting, and otherwise serves without idling. What can be said about its departure rate $\delta$?
options: $\delta=\mu$, since in an overloaded queue without blocking the output equals the capacity
$\delta=\lambda$, since without blocking every arriving job eventually leaves the system
$\delta<\mu$, since the server stands idle while jobs are waiting during its pauses
$\mu$ drops to the rate achieved with pauses, and $\delta$ equals this reduced $\mu$

questions.question: For a single server without blocking, empty at time $0$, the long-run arrival, departure and service rates $\lambda$, $\delta$, $\mu$ exist and are finite and positive, and it is observed that $\delta=\mu$. What can be concluded about $\lambda$?
options: $\lambda>\mu$, so the number of jobs in the system grows without bound
$\lambda\leq\mu$, since the output can reach $\mu$ only when the server keeps up
Nothing at all, because the service rate does not depend on the arrival stream
$\lambda\geq\mu$, but $\lambda=\mu$ is possible, so the queue need not grow

questions.question: A single server processes work at speed $\mu(i)=2$ units of work per time unit. Each job requires work $s_k=2$ or $s_k=4$ units, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, independently. What is the service rate of this server, in jobs per time unit?

A repair shop has two mechanics working in parallel: mechanic A has mean service time $10$ minutes per job and mechanic B $15$ minutes per job. What is the capacity of the shop, the number of jobs per hour the two could complete if they never stood idle?
